topic: Word Swap (Verbal Ability and Reading Comprehension)

sections.title: Basic Concept of Word Swap
sections.content: In a Word Swap question, two words in a sentence are placed in the wrong positions. By exchanging these two words, the sentence becomes grammatically correct and meaningful. The task is to identify the incorrect pair of words and swap them so that both grammar and meaning of the sentence become correct.

sections.title: Basic Subject-Verb Agreement
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the subject (the person or thing performing the action). Step 2: Check whether the verb is singular or plural. Step 3: If it seems incorrect, see whether swapping it with another verb in the sentence fixes the agreement. Example: 'The students studies hard and the teacher study them carefully.' Swapping 'studies' and 'study' makes the sentence correct.

sections.title: Adjective-Noun Pairing
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the adjective (the word describing a noun). Step 2: Check whether the adjective is paired with the correct noun. Step 3: If the meaning sounds odd, swap the adjective with another one that better matches the noun. Example: 'She wore a delicious dress and ate a beautiful cake.' Swapping 'delicious' and 'beautiful' corrects the meaning.

sections.title: Contextual Mismatch
sections.content: Step 1: Understand the overall meaning of the sentence. Step 2: Identify words that do not fit the context. Step 3: Swap them and check whether the sentence becomes logical. Example: 'The sun shines at night while the moon rises in the day.' Swapping 'night' and 'day' makes the sentence logically correct.

sections.title: Logical Flow Check
sections.content: Step 1: Read the sentence carefully and understand the general meaning. Step 2: Identify the word that breaks the logical flow. Step 3: Swap it with another word to see whether the sentence becomes smoother and more logical.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Swapping words without reading the entire sentence. 2. Checking only grammar and ignoring meaning. 3. Swapping words that are already correct.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: In Word Swap questions, two incorrectly placed words must be exchanged to make the sentence correct. Checking subject-verb agreement, adjective-noun pairing, and logical context is the most effective approach.

tricks.title: Grammar First Trick
tricks.explanation: First check the subject and verb because many swaps occur there.
tricks.example: The players plays well → swapping 'plays' and 'play' can correct the sentence.

tricks.title: Meaning Check Trick
tricks.explanation: If the sentence sounds strange, look for a contextual mismatch.
tricks.example: Cold fire or hot ice combinations usually indicate an incorrect pairing.

tricks.title: Adjective Pair Trick
tricks.explanation: An adjective must match the noun it describes.
tricks.example: Sweet song and melodious cake is an incorrect pairing.

tricks.title: Swap and Read Method
tricks.explanation: Swap the suspected words and read the sentence again to check if it sounds natural.
tricks.example: If the sentence flows smoothly after swapping, it is likely correct.

tricks.title: Elimination Trick
tricks.explanation: Eliminate the words that already appear correct and focus on the incorrect pair.
tricks.example: First identify the correct noun-verb pairs.

tricks.title: Context Clue Trick
tricks.explanation: Other words in the sentence often provide clues about which word is misplaced.
tricks.example: Rain is logically associated with umbrella.

tricks.title: Noun Relationship Trick
tricks.explanation: Sometimes two nouns are misplaced and swapping them clarifies the meaning.
tricks.example: Teacher teaches students, students learn from teacher.

tricks.title: Quick Logic Trick
tricks.explanation: If both grammar and meaning become correct after swapping, that is the correct answer.
tricks.example: Always check whether the sentence sounds natural.
